To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of chromosomal deletion(s), which may cause genetic disease, is high in human euploid embryos produced by IVF.
all human eupoid blastocysts with detectable chromosomal deletions are abnormal and transfer may cause birth defects, developmental and/or intellectual disability.
chromosomal deletions in human blastocyst can cause developmental delay or intellectual disabilities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prevalence of chromosomal deletion(s), which is the most common type of structural anomalies in human euploid embryos.
the clinical application of the chromosomal deletion(s), which is the first study to investigate the clinical significance of the deletions in human blastocyst using DNA microarray.
human embryo development, which will benefit human reproduction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the embryos with chromosal deletion should not be transferred, or at least further gene map and phenotype seeking should be conducted before making a final transfer decision.
all human blastocysts with deletions should not be transferred.
the chromosomal deletion(s), especially the deletion(s) that is/are related to developmental delay or intellectual disabilities should not be transferred.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chromosomal deletion in human blastocyst is not a benign anomaly.
the chromosomal deletions in human blastocyst are not benign and the transfer of these embryos to patients should be avoided.
the chromosomal deletion(s), which are detected by DNA microarray, should be avoided during preimplantation genetic screening (PGS) and/or genetic diagnosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
all human euploids with chromosomal deletion are not normal, but abnormal.

the embryos with chromosomally deleted regions should not be transferred, or the patients should be informed that the embryos may have a risk of developmental delay or intellectual disabilities, which is the first report to our knowledge.
the deletion size of the chromosomal deletion is important to the gene map and phenotype seeking.
